Native engine book, chapter 3: constrained estimation

Source: vignettes/articles/native-book-3-constraints.qmd

Chapters 1 and 2 minimized the discrepancy over all parameters. This chapter adds constraints such as a + b == 1.2 or cp == a*b and follows one fit through every stage the engine runs: turning a constraint into a row, handing the rows to the solver, judging the solution with the acceptance gate, polishing it, and handling rows that repeat each other.

You need Chapters 1 and 2; the short primers below introduce the needed calculus and optimization ideas
You get the constraint rows the engine builds, a trace of the solver, the three checks of the acceptance gate with a failing example of each, the Newton polish derived and reproduced by hand, and the redundant-row rules shown on real fits
Time about 50 minutes 
library(medfit)

Attaching package: 'medfit'
The following object is masked from 'package:stats':

    decompose
rd <- function(x, d = 4) round(x, d)
sci <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
d <- mediation_demo
model <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment
"

# Rebuild what fit_sem() builds before it optimizes: the parsed model, the RAM
# specification, the sample object and the constraint rows.
build <- function(text, data = d) {
  parsed <- medfit:::.sem_parse(text)
  tab <- medfit:::.sem_complete(parsed$parameters, NULL)
  conv <- medfit:::.sem_to_ram(tab)
  ram <- conv$ram
  smp <- medfit:::.sem_sample(data[, ram$obs], ram)
  list(ram = ram, smp = smp, cons = medfit:::.sem_constraint_rows(parsed$constraints, ram))
}

We use the same three-variable model throughout (no means, so the parameters are three paths and three variances). The unconstrained fit is saturated, with \(\text{df} = 0\). Every constraint below therefore costs one degree of freedom per independent equality.

1. From a constraint line to a row

First, picture the optimization. An optimizer tries parameter values and seeks the lowest discrepancy \(F\) (the model’s measure of disagreement with the data). In a two-parameter sketch, let \(F(a,b)=(a-1)^2+4(b-2)^2\); \(a\) and \(b\) are adjustable numbers. At \((a,b)=(0,0)\), \(F=17\). Its gradient \(\nabla F=(-2(a-1),8(b-2))=(-2,-16)\) gives the local slope in each direction. Its Hessian \(H=\operatorname{diag}(2,8)\) records how those slopes change: the \(b\) direction bends four times as strongly as the \(a\) direction. A shallow direction needs more movement to produce the same change in \(F\), and a nearly flat direction makes an optimum harder to locate reliably. This sketch is general math; the native engine minimizes its own \(F_{ML}\), defined in Chapter 1, using gradients and curvature checks (R/sem-optim.R).

What to remember: the gradient points uphill; the Hessian describes how the slope bends.

A constraint narrows the search. The feasible set is every parameter choice that obeys the rule. For example, \(c(a,b)=a+b-1\leq0\) permits \((0.2,0.3)\) because \(c=-0.5\); this constraint is inactive there. At \((0.4,0.6)\), \(c=0\), so the rule is active: a step increasing the sum would leave the feasible set. Here \(c\) is the signed constraint value and zero marks its boundary. medfit stores inequalities in this \(c\leq0\) direction (R/sem-constraints.R).

What to remember: inactive means slack remains; active means the point touches the boundary.

A constraint line has two sides, a comparison and labels of free parameters. The engine turns each line into the vector \(c(\theta) = \text{lhs} - \text{rhs}\) and a sense: an equality \(c(\theta) = 0\) or an inequality, always stored in the form \(c(\theta) \le 0\) (a > constraint is negated).

Linear constraints

Why normalize rows? A rule such as \(a+b=1\) describes the same set as \(2a+2b=2\), yet its raw coefficients are twice as large in the second writing. Their row lengths are \(\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt2\). Dividing each coefficient and constant by its row length gives the same unit-length row in both cases. Here a row is the list of coefficients multiplying the parameters. This general normalization explains the engine’s linear-row representation below.

What to remember: unit-length rows keep a repeated rule from changing scale merely because it was rewritten.

If \(c\) is linear in the parameters, \(c(\theta) = a^\top\theta + b\), so two kinds of evaluation recover its pieces: \(b = c(0)\) and, for each parameter \(k\), \(a_k = c(e_k) - c(0)\) with \(e_k\) the \(k\)th unit vector. The engine does exactly this with its expression evaluator, then divides \(a\) and \(b\) by the length of \(a\). After that, \(a\) has unit length, so the value of the row at \(\theta\) is the signed distance from \(\theta\) to the constraint’s hyperplane, and the tolerances that act on the rows themselves (the rank of the equality rows, and the test for implied inequalities in Section 5) mean the same thing for every constraint, however it was written. (The acceptance gate of Section 3 measures the distance in natural units instead, rescaling each row again.)

lin <- build(paste0(model, "a + b == 1.2\ncp < a\n"))
lin$ram$par_names
[1] "a"                    "b"                    "cp"
[4] "mediator1~~mediator1" "outcome~~outcome"     "treatment~~treatment"
lin$cons$eq
$A
          [,1]      [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
[1,] 0.7071068 0.7071068    0    0    0    0

$b
[1] -0.8485281

$text
[1] "a + b == 1.2"
lin$cons$ineq
$A
           [,1] [,2]      [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
[1,] -0.7071068    0 0.7071068    0    0    0

$b
[1] 0

$text
[1] "cp < a"

Check the first row by hand. The labels a and b are parameters here, so write the row’s pieces out in words. For a + b == 1.2, \(c(\theta) = \theta_a + \theta_b - 1.2\): the row vector has 1 in the columns of a and b and 0 elsewhere, and the constant is \(-1.2\). The row vector’s length is \(\sqrt 2\) = 1.4142, so the normalized row is 0.7071 in the columns of a and b with constant -0.8485, which is what the table shows. The second line, cp < a, is \(c(\theta) = \theta_{cp} - \theta_a \le 0\): it has \(-1\) at a and \(+1\) at cp, divided by \(\sqrt 2\).

An inequality line with a single label and a number (cp < 0.3) is not a row: the parser stores it as a bound on the parameter, which the solver handles separately. (An equality such as a == 1 stays a row.) The rows are empty and the bound is set:

bnd_text <- paste0(model, "cp < 0.3\n")
bnd <- build(bnd_text)
bnd_conv <- medfit:::.sem_to_ram(medfit:::.sem_complete(medfit:::.sem_parse(bnd_text)$parameters, NULL))
c(constraint_lines = nrow(medfit:::.sem_parse(bnd_text)$constraints), upper_bound_of_cp = bnd_conv$upper[["cp"]])
 constraint_lines upper_bound_of_cp
              0.0               0.3

Nonlinear constraints

cp == a*b is not linear. The engine keeps \(c(\theta) = cp - ab\) as a function (a closure over a checked expression tree) and evaluates its gradient by central differences at every point, with step \(\epsilon^{1/3}\max(|\theta_k|, u_k)\), where \(\epsilon\) is the machine precision and \(u_k\) the parameter’s natural unit (Section 2). The analytic gradient is \((-b, -a, 1)\) for \((a, b, cp)\), which gives something to check:

txt <- paste0(model, "cp == a*b\n")
nlb <- build(txt)
fit <- fit_sem(txt, d)
theta <- fit@theta
unit <- medfit:::.sem_step_floor(nlb$ram, nlb$smp)
nl <- nlb$cons$nl
cat("row text:", nl$text, "\n")
row text: cp == a*b 
rbind(
  central_difference = nl$jac(theta, unit)[1, 1:3],
  analytic = c(-theta[["b"]], -theta[["a"]], 1)
) |>
  `colnames<-`(c("a", "b", "cp")) |>
  rd(6)
                           a         b cp
central_difference -0.683163 -0.338117  1
analytic           -0.683163 -0.338117  1
c(value_at_solution = nl$value(theta))
value_at_solution
    -5.551115e-17

The central difference reproduces the analytic gradient to six decimals, and the constraint holds at the solution (the value is zero to rounding).

A product that is set to zero (a*b == 0) is a special case. The set where it holds is two lines, \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\), that cross at \(a = b = 0\). There the gradient \((b, a)\) is zero and the constraint qualification of Section 5 fails. Away from the crossing a local solver follows the branch nearest its start and can stop on the worse one, a local optimum. The engine therefore fits one linear model per factor (a == 0, b == 0), each from the default start, and keeps the one with the smaller discrepancy, a rule Chapter 5 puts to use. The two branches here give two different minima:

For several zero-product constraints, it tries each combination of factors, up to 64 branches; more than 64 is an error. Each branch starts cleanly, so one branch cannot inherit an infeasible point from another.

zp <- fit_sem(paste0(model, "a*b == 0\n"), d)
branch_f <- c(`a == 0` = fit_sem(paste0(model, "a == 0\n"), d)@f,
              `b == 0` = fit_sem(paste0(model, "b == 0\n"), d)@f)
branch_f
    a == 0     b == 0
0.04389351 0.40513506 
data.frame(chosen_branch = zp@internals$branch, discrepancy = zp@f)
  chosen_branch discrepancy
1        a == 0  0.04389351

Counting what a constraint removes

An equality removes one free parameter when its gradient is independent of the others’. The number removed is the rank of the equality gradients: stack them in a matrix and count its independent rows. The degrees of freedom are \(\text{moments} - (q - \text{rank})\):

fit_lin <- fit_sem(paste0(model, "a + b == 1.2\n"), d)
data.frame(
  model = c("no constraint", "a + b == 1.2", "cp == a*b"),
  q = c(length(fit_sem(model, d)@theta), length(fit_lin@theta), length(fit@theta)),
  rank_removed = c(0, fit_lin@internals$eq_rank, fit@internals$eq_rank),
  df = c(fit_sem(model, d)@df, fit_lin@df, fit@df)
)
          model q rank_removed df
1 no constraint 6            0  0
2  a + b == 1.2 6            1  1
3     cp == a*b 6            1  1

2. The solver

Why change units? In the general calculation \(x_k=\theta_k/u_k\), \(\theta_k\) is parameter \(k\), \(u_k>0\) is its natural unit, and \(x_k\) is its unitless working coordinate. For two parameters \(\theta=(0.2,200)\) with \(u=(1,1000)\), \(x=(0.2,0.2)\): a change of \(0.1\) in either \(x\) coordinate is one tenth of that parameter’s natural unit. The rule \(a+b/1000=0.4\) becomes \(x_1+x_2=0.4\); its normal vector \((1,1)\) has length \(\sqrt2\), so the unit-length row is \((x_1+x_2-0.4)/\sqrt2\). At \(x=(0.2,0.1)\) its signed value is \(-0.07071068\). A tolerance on this normalized distance has a common meaning across the two coordinates. medfit obtains the \(u_k\) from .sem_step_floor() and checks constraint distance in natural units (R/sem-constraints.R).

What to remember: scale parameters first, then compare constraint distances on one scale.

The engine minimizes \(F_{ML}(\theta)\) subject to the rows with SLSQP, the sequential least-squares quadratic programming algorithm of Kraft, as implemented in the NLopt library and called through the nloptr package. At each iterate SLSQP forms a quadratic model of the objective (the gradient plus a quasi-Newton approximation of the curvature of the Lagrangian) and linearizes the constraints. It then solves that small quadratic program for a step and chooses a step length by a line search on a merit function that penalizes constraint violation.

Two engine choices matter to what follows.

Natural units. SLSQP works on \(x = \theta / u\) with \(u_k\) the parameter’s natural unit (.sem_step_floor()): the standard deviation of the target over that of the source for a path, the product of the two standard deviations for a (co)variance. The objective, gradient and constraint rows are mapped into \(x\) (a linear row \(a^\top\theta + b\) becomes the row \((a \odot u)^\top x + b\)), and the solution is mapped back. A step of size 1 then means about the same in every parameter, whatever the units of the data.

rd(stats::setNames(unit, nlb$ram$par_names), 3)
                   a                    b                   cp
               2.200                1.221                2.686
mediator1~~mediator1     outcome~~outcome treatment~~treatment
               1.210                1.804                0.250

Defaults. The first start is moment based (.sem_default_start(): paths at 10% of the natural unit, variances at half the variable’s variance, covariances at 0). Tolerances are xtol_rel = 1e-10 and ftol_rel = 1e-12.

A trace shows the iterations. We call the solver directly with a wrapper that records each evaluation of the objective together with the constraint violation, from the default start:

ram <- nlb$ram
smp <- nlb$smp
cons <- nlb$cons
lb <- rep(-Inf, ram$q)
ub <- rep(Inf, ram$q)
start <- medfit:::.sem_default_start(ram, smp)
obj <- medfit:::.sem_objective(ram, smp)
opts <- list(algorithm = "NLOPT_LD_SLSQP", xtol_rel = 1e-10, ftol_rel = 1e-12, maxeval = 10000L)
trace_env <- new.env()
trace_env$rows <- list()
f_traced <- function(x) {
  value <- obj$f(x * unit)
  trace_env$rows[[length(trace_env$rows) + 1L]] <- c(objective = value, violation = abs(cons$nl$value(x * unit)))
  value
}
run <- medfit:::.sem_nlopt(
  start / unit, f_traced, function(x) obj$g(x * unit) * unit, lb / unit, ub / unit, opts,
  constraints = medfit:::.sem_nlopt_constraints(cons, unit)
)
tr <- do.call(rbind, trace_env$rows)
solution <- run$solution * unit
cat("status", run$status, "after", run$iterations, "iterations and", nrow(tr), "evaluations\n")
status 3 after 22 iterations and 24 evaluations
signif(tr[c(1:6, nrow(tr) - 3:0), ], 3)
      objective violation
 [1,]    1.0800  2.42e-01
 [2,]    1.0800  2.42e-01
 [3,]    1.0800  2.42e-01
 [4,]    2.1400  2.10e+00
 [5,]    0.4240  3.19e-01
 [6,]    0.4240  3.19e-01
 [7,]    0.0105  1.19e-09
 [8,]    0.0105  2.99e-12
 [9,]    0.0105  6.19e-15
[10,]    0.0105  0.00e+00

Rows that repeat one another are repeated evaluations at the same point (the nloptr wrapper evaluates the start once to check the objective’s return type, and the solver evaluates some points twice). The trace starts at a point that violates the constraint (violation is \(|cp - ab|\)), the violation falls by many orders of magnitude over the last evaluations, and the objective settles at 0.0104708. The run ended with NLopt status 3; the engine treats the codes 1 (generic success), 3 (the objective stopped changing, ftol_rel) and 4 (the parameters stopped moving, xtol_rel) as successes.

Local versus global. A local optimum wins against nearby feasible points; a global optimum wins against every feasible point. In a two-parameter general-math sketch, minimize \(F(a,b)=(a-1)^2+(b-2)^2\) subject to \(ab=0\). The branch \(a=0\) has best point \((0,2)\) and \(F=1\); the branch \(b=0\) has best point \((1,0)\) and \(F=4\). Each wins on its own branch, but only \(F=1\) wins globally. Multiple starts can reveal such disagreement; agreement alone cannot prove that an unexplored branch is worse. medfit records the comparison in diagnostics$optimum (R/sem-optim.R).

What to remember: several agreeing starts provide evidence; only a valid lower bound certifies the global minimum.

Several starts. A nonlinear constraint can have several local optima (a*b > 0.1 is feasible on two separate regions), so for such a model the engine runs every start (the default one and up to n_starts - 1 perturbed ones, drawn under a fixed seed derived from the model) and keeps the accepted solution with the lowest discrepancy, warning if the accepted ones disagree. The attempts of this fit, from the engine’s own optimizer:

o <- medfit:::.sem_optimize(ram, smp, start, constraints = cons)
attempts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(o$attempts), function(i) {
  a <- o$attempts[[i]]
  data.frame(start = i, status = a$status, accepted = a$accepted, discrepancy = a$f,
             decrement = signif(a$decrement, 2))
}))
attempts
   start status accepted discrepancy decrement
1      1      3     TRUE  0.01047077   6.5e-14
2      2      3     TRUE  0.01047077   1.1e-13
3      3      3     TRUE  0.01047077   3.5e-14
4      4      3     TRUE  0.01047077   7.0e-14
5      5      3     TRUE  0.01047077   2.4e-14
6      6      3     TRUE  0.01047077   1.0e-14
7      7      3     TRUE  0.01047077   4.8e-14
8      8      3     TRUE  0.01047077   4.3e-15
9      9      3     TRUE  0.01047077   8.3e-16
10    10      3     TRUE  0.01047077   5.4e-16
11    11      3     TRUE  0.01047077   5.5e-15
12    12      3     TRUE  0.01047077   7.1e-15
13    13      3     TRUE  0.01047077   5.5e-14

All 13 starts are accepted and reach the same discrepancy (the largest spread is 8.9e-16), so no warning is raised.

For nonlinear rows, inspect fit@diagnostics$optimum as well as the acceptance gate. Its status is unique when the best-of-starts comparison does not apply, certified when a feasible fit without the nonlinear rows supplies the lower bound on discrepancy, agreed when several accepted starts agree within 1e-6, disagreed when they do not, and single when only one start is accepted. The record also gives n_starts, n_accepted, spread, best_of and certified. agreed and single do not establish a global optimum; a better basin may remain. Increase n_starts when that matters, especially after a disagreed or single verdict.

For a nonlinear row, the engine also tries the unconstrained estimate and sign-flipped path starts, since a product constraint can separate sign branches. Variances named in those rows have a solver floor of 1e-4 times their natural unit. An active floor warns that the constrained optimum may be improper. These safeguards apply only to models with nonlinear rows.

3. The acceptance gate

Why check beyond the solver’s stop message? A small change in \(F\) can mean either “at the bottom” or “walking along a nearly flat slope.” For the earlier \(F(a,b)\) at \((0,0)\), the \(a\) slope is \(-2\), so increasing \(a\) lowers \(F\) despite a smaller slope than the \(b\) slope \(-16\). The gate therefore checks feasibility, curvature, and remaining improvement (R/sem-constraints.R).

What to remember: a stop code records why the algorithm stopped, not whether the point is an optimum.

A solver can stop for reasons that have nothing to do with having found the optimum. The engine therefore accepts a solution only if it passes three checks, in this order (besides guards against a non-finite Hessian, an implied covariance that is not positive definite, and a nearly singular reduced Hessian):

  1. the solver status is a success code (1, 3 or 4);
  2. every constraint holds to \(10^{-6}\) in natural units;
  3. the Newton decrement on the active-constraint null space is at most \(10^{-3}\), with a positive definite reduced Hessian whose smallest Jacobi-scaled eigenvalue is at least \(10^{-4}\).

For curved rows, the active Jacobian is recomputed at the candidate point, not reused from the start. The reduced curvature includes the Lagrangian Hessian: the objective Hessian plus multiplier-weighted constraint Hessians, whose entries come from central differences of the row Jacobians.

Check 3 needs a derivation. We build it in four steps.

Multipliers before the matrix algebra. For general math, minimize \(F(a)=(a-2)^2\) under \(c(a)=a-1\leq0\). At the active point \(a=1\), \(F'(1)=-2\) and \(c'(1)=1\). The Lagrangian \(L(a,\lambda)=F(a)+\lambda c(a)\) has slope \(-2+\lambda=0\), so the multiplier is \(\lambda=2\geq0\). It measures the benefit of loosening this upper limit: increasing the limit by a small amount can lower the best \(F\) by about twice that amount. For an inactive inequality the multiplier is zero; together with feasibility, stationarity, and \(\lambda c=0\), these are the first-order KKT conditions. For a wrong-sign example, minimize \(F(a)=a^2\) at the same boundary \(a=1\): \(F'(1)=2\) gives \(\lambda=-2\). Moving inward to \(a<1\) lowers \(F\), so this active point is not a constrained minimum. With the \(c\leq0\) convention, a negative multiplier does not mean that loosening the upper limit lowers the optimal \(F\); it means releasing the claim that this boundary must stay active allows an improving feasible move. medfit checks inequality signs as a warning, with an active-bound inward-slope rejection (R/sem-constraints.R).

What to remember: for \(c\leq0\), an active minimum needs a nonnegative inequality multiplier.

Only allowed directions count. In the two-parameter sketch \(F(a,b)=(a-1)^2+4(b-2)^2\), impose the active equality \(a=0\). Its Jacobian row is \(M=(1,0)\); \(Mp=0\) requires a feasible small move \(p=(0,t)\), where \(t\) is any number. A null-space basis is \(Z=(0,1)^\top\). The objective Hessian is \(H=\operatorname{diag}(2,8)\), so the reduced Hessian is \(H_r=Z^\top HZ=8\): curvature in the forbidden \(a\) direction does not enter. At \((a,b)=(0,1.9)\), the reduced gradient is \(g_r=Z^\top\nabla F=-0.8\). The Newton decrement is \(\sqrt{g_r^\top H_r^{-1}g_r}=\sqrt{0.8^2/8}=0.2828427\). This is the dimensionless remaining-improvement number the medfit gate compares with \(10^{-3}\); this point fails. For curved rows the gate instead uses the Lagrangian’s Hessian, as derived below (R/sem-constraints.R).

What to remember: project onto feasible directions, then compare the decrement with \(10^{-3}\).

Why scale the curvature test? Jacobi scaling divides Hessian entry \(H_{ij}\) by \(\sqrt{H_{ii}H_{jj}}\), where \(i,j\) name coordinates with positive diagonal curvature. For \(H=\operatorname{diag}(2,200)\), the scaled matrix is the identity and both eigenvalues are 1, although the raw curvatures differ by a factor of 100. A near-flat coupled example is \(H=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0.99999\\0.99999&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\): its smallest scaled eigenvalue is \(0.00001\). An eigenvalue measures curvature along a special direction; a value near zero means the curvature test cannot reliably separate that direction from a flat one. medfit rejects a reduced Hessian whose smallest Jacobi-scaled eigenvalue is below \(10^{-4}\) (R/sem-constraints.R).

What to remember: scaling removes individual coordinate units before testing for near-flat curvature.

Step 1: the stationarity condition. At a constrained minimum with active rows \(M\) (the Jacobian of the active constraints, one row each), the gradient \(g\) of the objective is a combination of the constraint gradients: \(g + M^\top\lambda = 0\), the Lagrange condition, with \(\lambda\) the multipliers. Equivalently, \(g\) has no component along any direction \(p\) that keeps the constraints, \(M p = 0\).

Step 2: the null space. Let \(Z\) be a matrix whose orthonormal columns span the null space of \(M\): every feasible direction is \(p = Z w\). The reduced gradient is \(g_r = Z^\top g\), which is zero at a constrained stationary point.

Step 3: the curvature along the constraints. For a linear constraint the second derivative of the objective along \(Z\) is \(H_r = Z^\top H Z\) with \(H\) the Hessian of the objective. For a curved constraint the constraint itself bends, and the right curvature is that of the Lagrangian, \(H_L = H + \sum_i \lambda_i \nabla^2 c_i\) over the active nonlinear rows, so \(H_r = Z^\top H_L Z\). (Reason: along a curve \(\theta(t)\) that stays on the constraint, the second derivative of the objective is \(\dot\theta^\top H \dot\theta + g^\top \ddot\theta\), and the Lagrange condition \(g = -M^\top\lambda\) turns the second term into \(-\lambda^\top M \ddot\theta\), which the curvature of the constraint, \(\ddot c = 0 = M\ddot\theta + \dot\theta^\top \nabla^2 c\,\dot\theta\), converts to \(+\lambda\,\dot\theta^\top\nabla^2 c\,\dot\theta\).)

Step 4: the Newton decrement. A second-order model of the objective along the null space is \(q(w) = g_r^\top w + \tfrac12 w^\top H_r w\). If \(H_r\) is positive definite its minimum is at \(w^\star = -H_r^{-1} g_r\) and the predicted decrease in the objective is \(\tfrac12 g_r^\top H_r^{-1} g_r\). The Newton decrement is

\[ \lambda_N = \sqrt{g_r^\top H_r^{-1} g_r} , \]

the size of the remaining gradient measured in the units of the curvature. It does not depend on the units of the parameters. Rescale them, \(\theta = D\xi\) with \(D\) diagonal. Then the gradient becomes \(D g\), the Hessian \(D H D\) and the constraint rows \(M D\) (chain rule), so the feasible directions become \(D^{-1}\) times the old ones. The quadratic form \(g^\top Z (Z^\top H Z)^{-1} Z^\top g\) is the same for every basis \(Z\) of one subspace (another basis is \(Z R\) with \(R\) invertible, and the \(R\) factors cancel), and substituting \(D g\), \(D H D\) and the basis \(D^{-1} Z\) cancels every \(D\): for example, without constraints \((D g)^\top (D H D)^{-1} (D g) = g^\top H^{-1} g\). So one threshold, \(10^{-3}\), works whatever the units of the data.

We compute each piece for our fit. The helper .sem_active_set() returns the active rows in natural units, the constraint distance, and the null-space basis \(Z\) (from a singular value decomposition of the normalized active rows):

act <- medfit:::.sem_active_set(theta, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
gate <- medfit:::.sem_gate(theta, 3L, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
cat("active rows:", act$text[act$active_row], "\n")
active rows: cp == a*b 
cat("constraint distance (natural units):", signif(act$dist, 3), "\n")
constraint distance (natural units): 1.79e-17 
cat("null space basis Z:", nrow(act$z), "x", ncol(act$z), "(6 parameters, 1 active row)\n")
null space basis Z: 6 x 5 (6 parameters, 1 active row)
x_grad <- medfit:::.sem_grad(theta, ram, smp) * act$u
x_hess <- medfit:::.sem_hess_f(theta, ram, smp) * outer(act$u, act$u)
lagrangian <- medfit:::.sem_lagrangian_hessian(x_hess, x_grad, act, cons, theta)
active_rows <- act$ax[act$active_row, , drop = FALSE]
multiplier <- qr.solve(t(active_rows), -x_grad)
cat("multiplier from g + M' lambda = 0:", rd(multiplier, 4), "\n")
multiplier from g + M' lambda = 0: -0.0742 
reduced_gradient <- crossprod(act$z, x_grad)
cat("size of the reduced gradient:", signif(sqrt(sum(reduced_gradient^2)), 3), "\n")
size of the reduced gradient: 1.2e-13 
rbind(objective_hessian_only = eigen(crossprod(act$z, x_hess %*% act$z))$values,
      with_lagrangian_term = eigen(crossprod(act$z, lagrangian %*% act$z))$values) |> rd(3)
                        [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4] [,5]
objective_hessian_only 3.305 2.396 2.092 1.076    1
with_lagrangian_term   3.408 2.360 1.999 1.075    1

At the optimum the reduced gradient is zero (the Lagrange condition holds with a nonzero multiplier, because the constraint is binding), so the decrement is zero. The last table lists the eigenvalues of the reduced Hessian built two ways. Both are positive, so this point passes the second-order test either way, but the numbers differ: the Lagrangian term \(\lambda\nabla^2 c\) changes the curvature along the curved constraint, and the engine uses the version with it. On a different problem the two can disagree about the sign of an eigenvalue, and then only the second is right (the objective’s Hessian alone can call a saddle point of the constrained problem a minimum).

The gate’s own verdict combines all of this. Here it is, together with three solutions that should be rejected, one for each check:

show <- function(g) data.frame(accepted = g$accepted, decrement = signif(g$decrement, 3), reason = g$reason)
# 1. a good solution
good <- medfit:::.sem_gate(theta, 3L, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
# 2. a feasible point that is not the optimum: move a, then put cp back on the curve cp = a * b
off <- theta
off["a"] <- off["a"] + 0.05
off["cp"] <- off["a"] * off["b"]
off_gate <- medfit:::.sem_gate(off, 3L, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
# 3. an infeasible point
broken <- theta
broken["cp"] <- broken["cp"] + 0.1
broken_gate <- medfit:::.sem_gate(broken, 3L, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
# 4. a good point with a failure status from the solver
status_gate <- medfit:::.sem_gate(theta, -4L, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
verdicts <- rbind(optimum = show(good), `feasible, not optimal` = show(off_gate), infeasible = show(broken_gate),
                  `bad solver status` = show(status_gate))
verdicts
                      accepted decrement
optimum                   TRUE  6.51e-14
feasible, not optimal    FALSE  3.96e-02
infeasible               FALSE        NA
bad solver status        FALSE        NA
                                                                               reason
optimum
feasible, not optimal                             stationarity 3.96e-02 exceeds 1e-03
infeasible            constraint 'cp == a*b' is violated by 3.22e-02 in natural units
bad solver status                              nloptr status -4 is not a success code

(A fourth check examines multiplier signs. For an active inequality, a wrong sign warns: dependent active rows can make individual multipliers ambiguous. For an active bound, a gradient pointing into the feasible interior rejects the point, because moving inward would lower the objective.) Each failing point is rejected for the right reason. The second one satisfies the constraint exactly and is rejected only because its decrement is large: that is the stationarity check doing its job.

Finally the scale-invariance claim. Multiply outcome by 1000. The model keeps its form, because cp == a*b is preserved when \(b\) and \(cp\) are both multiplied by 1000 (so \(cp' = 1000\,cp = a \cdot 1000\,b = a b'\)). Map the feasible but non-optimal point of the last test to the new scale (\(b\) and \(cp\) times 1000, the residual variance of outcome times \(10^6\)), build the new model on the rescaled data, and compare the decrements:

d_big <- d
d_big$outcome <- d_big$outcome * 1000
big <- build(txt, d_big)
off_big <- off
off_big[c("b", "cp")] <- off_big[c("b", "cp")] * 1000
off_big["outcome~~outcome"] <- off_big["outcome~~outcome"] * 1000^2
gate_big <- medfit:::.sem_gate(off_big, 3L, big$ram, big$smp, lb, ub, big$cons)
c(original_data = off_gate$decrement, outcome_times_1000 = gate_big$decrement)
     original_data outcome_times_1000
        0.03958072         0.03958072

The two decrements are the same number, although the parameters differ by factors up to \(10^6\): the gate works in natural units, which rescale with the data, so its verdict does not depend on the units of the data.

4. The Newton polish

SLSQP stops when the objective changes by less than ftol_rel, and along a flat stretch of a curved constraint that can happen a little before the true optimum. Our solver run did just that:

cat("distance of the SLSQP solution from the exact optimum:", signif(max(abs(solution - theta)), 3), "\n")
distance of the SLSQP solution from the exact optimum: 8.1e-06 
gate_raw <- medfit:::.sem_gate(solution, run$status, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
c(accepted = gate_raw$accepted, decrement = signif(gate_raw$decrement, 3),
  violation = signif(abs(cons$nl$value(solution)), 3))
 accepted decrement violation
 1.00e+00  8.80e-06  1.19e-09

The point passes the gate (its decrement is below \(10^{-3}\)) but is 8.1e-06 from the optimum in the largest coordinate. The engine then takes Newton steps on the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) system of the active set. We derive the step.

The KKT system. Look for a point \(x + \delta\) and multipliers \(\nu\) that satisfy the two conditions of a constrained stationary point, linearized at the current \(x\). Stationarity of the Lagrangian, \(g + H_L\,\delta + M^\top\nu = 0\) (the gradient of the Lagrangian expanded to first order in \(\delta\)), and feasibility of the active rows, \(c + M\delta = 0\) (the constraint expanded to first order). Stacked:

\[ \begin{pmatrix} H_L & M^\top \\ M & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \delta \\ \nu \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -g \\ -c \end{pmatrix} . \]

This is Newton’s method for the equations \(\nabla_x L = 0\), \(c = 0\), with one approximation: the multipliers \(\lambda\) inside \(H_L\) are estimated at the current point by least squares from \(g + M^\top\lambda = 0\), as in Section 3, and \(\nu\) is discarded after the step. Near the solution that estimate converges to the true multipliers, so the step does too. Solving the system gives a step that both reduces the gradient and moves back toward the constraint. We code it, and iterate from the SLSQP solution:

kkt_step <- function(th) {
  a <- medfit:::.sem_active_set(th, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
  g <- medfit:::.sem_grad(th, ram, smp) * a$u
  h <- medfit:::.sem_hess_f(th, ram, smp) * outer(a$u, a$u)
  hl <- medfit:::.sem_lagrangian_hessian(h, g, a, cons, th)
  m <- a$ax[a$active_row, , drop = FALSE]
  cval <- a$cval[a$active_row]
  k <- nrow(m)
  kkt <- rbind(cbind(hl, t(m)), cbind(m, matrix(0, k, k)))
  sol <- solve(kkt, c(-g, -cval))
  th + sol[seq_len(ram$q)] * a$u
}
path <- list(solution)
for (i in 1:4) path[[i + 1L]] <- kkt_step(path[[i]])
newton <- data.frame(
  iteration = 0:4,
  constraint_violation = vapply(path, function(t) signif(abs(cons$nl$value(t)), 3), numeric(1)),
  decrement = vapply(path, function(t) {
    signif(medfit:::.sem_gate(t, 3L, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)$decrement, 3)
  }, numeric(1)),
  distance_from_exact_optimum = vapply(path, function(t) signif(max(abs(t - theta)), 3), numeric(1))
)
newton
  iteration constraint_violation decrement distance_from_exact_optimum
1         0             1.19e-09  8.80e-06                    8.10e-06
2         1             3.28e-12  1.07e-10                    1.18e-10
3         2             2.78e-17  1.01e-13                    2.15e-13
4         3             2.78e-17  9.44e-14                    1.40e-13
5         4             5.55e-17  6.98e-15                    4.55e-14

The distance from the optimum falls from 8.1e-06 to 1.2e-10 in one step and to rounding error in the next, and the constraint violation and the decrement fall with it: Newton’s method converges quadratically near a solution, so the error is roughly squared at each step until it reaches rounding error. The engine’s own polish, .sem_polish(), adds safeguards (it takes at most 8 steps, keeps a step only while a merit function falls, refuses to move more than \(10^{-2}\) natural units, and gives up if the active set changes or the KKT matrix is singular), and its result is accepted only if the gate accepts it again and the discrepancy does not rise by more than \(10^{-8}\). It lands where our bare iteration does:

polished <- medfit:::.sem_polish(solution, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
c(polish_vs_my_iteration = max(abs(polished - path[[5]])),
  polish_vs_engine_fit = max(abs(polished - theta)),
  discrepancy_before = medfit:::.sem_fml(solution, ram, smp),
  discrepancy_after = medfit:::.sem_fml(polished, ram, smp))
polish_vs_my_iteration   polish_vs_engine_fit     discrepancy_before
          4.773959e-15           4.074519e-14           1.047077e-02
     discrepancy_after
          1.047077e-02

5. Redundant rows

What can a repeated rule do? In general math, \(a+b=1\) and \(2a+2b=2\) describe one rule: the second active gradient \((2,2)\) is twice the first \((1,1)\), so their two-row matrix has rank 1. The feasible set is well defined, but a solver that treats them as two independent directions cannot assign a unique pair of multipliers; its constraint step can stall. LICQ is the name for the requirement that active gradient rows be linearly independent. Changing the second rule to \(2a+2b=3\) instead makes the set empty. medfit sends an independent equality subset to SLSQP and still checks every original row (R/sem-constraints.R).

What to remember: duplicate active rows count once; contradictory rows remain a failure.

Constraint sets sometimes repeat themselves, and that is a problem for a solver. SLSQP assumes the active constraint gradients are linearly independent (the linear independence constraint qualification, LICQ); when two active rows are parallel it can stop with an error although the constraints are consistent. The engine therefore protects the solver in two ways.

Dependent equalities. The rows handed to the solver are an independent subset (chosen from a pivoted QR decomposition of the row matrix, which finds which rows add rank), while the acceptance gate still checks every row. So a harmless repeat is dropped, and a contradiction is still caught:

dup <- build(paste0(model, "a == b\nb == a\n"))
cat("rows built:", nrow(dup$cons$eq$A), "; independent rows sent to the solver:",
    nrow(medfit:::.sem_independent_rows(dup$cons$eq)$A), "; rank:", medfit:::.sem_eq_rank(dup$cons$eq), "\n")
rows built: 2 ; independent rows sent to the solver: 1 ; rank: 1 
fit_dup <- fit_sem(paste0(model, "a == b\nb == a\n"), d)
fit_one <- fit_sem(paste0(model, "a == b\n"), d)
c(df_duplicates = fit_dup@df, df_single = fit_one@df,
  largest_estimate_difference = max(abs(fit_dup@theta - fit_one@theta)))
              df_duplicates                   df_single
                          1                           1
largest_estimate_difference
                          0

The duplicated pair counts as one constraint (rank 1, so the degrees of freedom are the same as with one line) and the estimates are identical. Contradictory lines, by contrast, are reported by the gate (the error names the violated row):

contradiction <- tryCatch(fit_sem(paste0(model, "a == 1\na == 2\n"), d), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
contradiction
[1] "no start converged (5 tried); best attempt: status 3, stationarity NA; constraint 'a == 2' is violated by 4.54e-01 in natural units"

Implied inequalities. An inequality whose gradient lies in the span of the equality gradients has a constant value on the set where the equalities hold. If that constant satisfies it, the inequality is either active everywhere on that set or never active, and an everywhere-active row is another LICQ failure. Such a row is detected when its gradient lies within \(10^{-12}\) of the span of the independent equalities (the rows have unit length, so this is an angle), and it is dropped from the solver’s rows. The gate still checks it. We build the case a == b together with a < b, whose value on the equality set is exactly 0, and the case a + b == 0.8 with a + b < 0.9, whose value on the equality set is \(-0.1\) before normalization (never active):

drop_check <- function(text) {
  bb <- build(text)
  kept <- medfit:::.sem_drop_implied_ineq(bb$cons$ineq, medfit:::.sem_independent_rows(bb$cons$eq))
  c(inequality_rows_built = nrow(bb$cons$ineq$A), rows_sent_to_the_solver = nrow(kept$A))
}
dropped <- rbind(`a == b with a < b` = drop_check(paste0(model, "a == b\na < b\n")),
                 `a + b == 0.8 with a + b < 0.9` = drop_check(paste0(model, "a + b == 0.8\na + b < 0.9\n")))
dropped
                              inequality_rows_built rows_sent_to_the_solver
a == b with a < b                                 1                       0
a + b == 0.8 with a + b < 0.9                     1                       0
fit_imp <- fit_sem(paste0(model, "a == b\na < b\n"), d)
c(discrepancy_with_inequality = fit_imp@f, discrepancy_without = fit_one@f,
  largest_estimate_difference = max(abs(fit_imp@theta - fit_one@theta)))
discrepancy_with_inequality         discrepancy_without
                 0.01167511                  0.01167511
largest_estimate_difference
                 0.00000000 
fit_imp@diagnostics$active_constraints
[1] "a == b" "a < b"

The fit with the redundant inequality gives the same result as the fit without it, and active_constraints still lists both rows, so the gate knew about it. A row the equalities violate is not dropped: near-dependence does not prove the set is infeasible, so the solver is left to try and the gate reports the failure:

violated <- tryCatch(fit_sem(paste0(model, "a + b == 0.8\na + b < 0.5\n"), d), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
violated
[1] "no start converged (5 tried); best attempt: status -4, stationarity NA; nloptr status -4 is not a success code; constraint 'a + b < 0.5' is violated by 1.19e-01 in natural units"

6. The covariance of a constrained fit

The standard errors of Chapter 5 come from the information matrix. With active constraints the estimates cannot move in the directions that violate them, so the covariance must be zero in those directions. Near \(\hat\theta\) the feasible points are \(\theta = \hat\theta + Z w\) (to first order), with \(w\) unconstrained. In \(w\) the information is \(Z^\top I Z\) (chain rule, as in Chapter 2), so \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat w) \approx (Z^\top I Z)^{-1}\), and mapping back through \(\theta = \hat\theta + Z w\) replaces \(I^{-1}\) with

\[ V = Z\,(Z^\top I\, Z)^{-1} Z^\top , \]

with \(Z\) the null-space basis in \(\theta\) units (z_theta from .sem_active_set()). Compute it by hand from the expected information and compare with the covariance the engine reports for the same setting:

fit_exp <- fit_sem(txt, d, information = "expected")
info <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(fit_exp@theta, ram, smp, NULL)
act_exp <- medfit:::.sem_active_set(fit_exp@theta, ram, smp, lb, ub, cons)
zt <- act_exp$z_theta
v_hand <- zt %*% solve(t(zt) %*% info %*% zt) %*% t(zt)
c(difference_from_engine = max(abs(v_hand - fit_exp@vcov)), largest_entry = max(abs(v_hand)))
difference_from_engine          largest_entry
          8.673617e-19           8.211061e-03 
cat("rank of V:", qr(fit_exp@vcov, tol = 1e-10)$rank, "of", ram$q, "parameters\n")
rank of V: 5 of 6 parameters

\(V\) has rank 5 and not 6: with one binding equality the six estimates have five degrees of freedom of variation.

7. Cross-checks

lavaan accepts cp == a*b in the model text. OpenMx takes it as an algebra and a constraint. Both fit the same model, and we compare the chi-square, the degrees of freedom, the estimates and the standard errors, from the expected and from the observed information (the engine’s and lavaan’s must be set to the same one):

lv <- lavaan::sem(txt, d, fixed.x = FALSE, information = "expected")

   lavaan->lav_test_browne(): Browne's test is not available (yet) when

fit_obs <- fit_sem(txt, d, information = "observed")
data.frame(
  quantity = c("chisq", "df"),
  medfit = c(fit@n_obs * fit@f, fit@df),
  lavaan = c(lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "chisq"), lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "df"))
)

chisq    chisq 4.188307 4.188307
df          df 1.000000 1.000000

  se_difference_expected = max(abs(sqrt(diag(fit_exp@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv)))[nm])),
  se_difference_observed = max(abs(sqrt(diag(fit_obs@vcov)) - sqrt(diag(lavaan::vcov(lv_obs)))[nm])))

suppressMessages(library(OpenMx))
mxOption(NULL, "Number of Threads", 1)

vars <- names(dat)
mod <- mxModel(
  "constrained", type = "RAM", manifestVars = vars,
  mxPath(from = "treatment", to = "mediator1", values = 0.3, labels = "a"),
  mxPath(from = "mediator1", to = "outcome", values = 0.6, labels = "b"),

run_mx <- mxRun(mod, silent = TRUE)
est_mx <- stats::setNames(summary(run_mx)$parameters$Estimate, summary(run_mx)$parameters$name)

data.frame(quantity = "-2 log L", medfit = -2 * as.numeric(logLik(fit_mean)),
           OpenMx = summary(run_mx)$Minus2LogLikelihood)
  quantity  medfit  OpenMx
1 -2 log L 2980.31 2980.31
c(largest_estimate_difference = max(abs(est_mx[c("a", "b", "cp")] - fit@theta[c("a", "b", "cp")])))
largest_estimate_difference
               8.959096e-08

 a  b cp
NA NA NA

OpenMx’s -2 log L includes the means, which is why the native fit with a mean structure is the comparison. Its standard errors for the three parameters in the mxConstraint are printed last; when they are NA (OpenMx does not always report standard errors under a nonlinear equality), the standard errors are compared with lavaan only.

Check yourself

  1. Why do rows have unit length, and what would break if they did not? (Answer: the tolerances that act on the rows, the rank of the equality rows and the \(10^{-12}\) test for implied inequalities, would depend on how a constraint was written: 2*a + 2*b == 2.4 and a + b == 1.2 would be treated differently.)
  2. For a*b == 0.1, what is the gradient of the row at \(a = b = 0\)? Why is that not the problem it is for a*b == 0? (Answer: \((b, a) = 0\) there, but \(a = b = 0\) is infeasible for a*b == 0.1, whose feasible set, a hyperbola, has a nonzero gradient at every point. For a*b == 0 the point \(a = b = 0\) is feasible: it is where the two branches cross, and the solver can stop on either branch.)
  3. A fit is rejected with the reason stationarity ... exceeds 1e-03. Is the constraint satisfied? (Answer: yes, the constraint check comes first; the point is feasible but not yet an optimum, as in the feasible, not optimal row above.)
